name: wood
summary: A haft: a turned length of timber, gripped and knocked about, never finished.
why: Metallic 0.0. Wood is the plainest dielectric in this library and the one where getting
that wrong is most obvious - a metallic haft is a chrome rod with a woodgrain decal on
it, which is what MU's flat art becomes the moment a light hits it.
Roughness 0.72, the same as the leather wrap and for the same reason: both are a worn
surface a hand has been on, and neither has a sharp highlight anywhere along it. It has
not been swept - MU2/tests/materials.sh cannot sweep it, because the axe is three
materials and the tool scales a whole item - so it is a reasoned starting figure and is
flagged as one.
The grain is brushed and runs along the haft. Wood is the most directional surface here:
it is fibres laid the length of a branch, so a highlight travelling across one stretches
into a line the way it does on a rolled blade and unlike anything cast. Reusing the
brushed kind is not laziness about a fourth kind - it is the same fact about a surface,
which is that its structure runs one way.
Depth 0.08, down from a first guess of 0.22. At 0.22 the haft came out corrugated: hard
dark lines running its length, more like a fluted column than a piece of timber. Wood
grain is a colour variation far more than it is a relief - the fibres sit flush and only
the odd raised one catches a light - and MU's art already paints the colour part, so
what a normal map has left to add here is very little.
Coarser than steel's, still. Blade steel is 520 cells of mill grain that only shows at a
graze; timber's is visible from across a room, so this is 180. That and the depth are
the whole difference between the two brushed materials.
